                  https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/m7f8a
                  
                ")) found that more collectivist countries and regions (e.g., Hong Kong, Taiwan, and South Korea) have been more effective in containing the spread of the coronavirus compared to more individualistic countries (e.g., the United States, Spain, and Italy). Given the contrasting sociopolitical responses to the COVID-19 pandemic between China and the U.S., it is pertinent to understand how variations in Chinese and U.S. individuals’ trust in government and attitudes towards COVID-19 preventive measures may impact their pandemic behaviors and mental health outcomes in a time of uncertainty. Our study extends prior research to examine the specific cognitive processes (e.g., individual cognitive factors such as NFC), trust in government, and attitudes) on pandemic compliance behavior and mental health among participants in the U.S. and China. We hypothesized that:

H3a: There would be mean level differences in trust in government and attitudes towards preventive measures between Chinese and U.S. participants. Chinese participants would report more trust in government and more positive attitudes towards preventive measures than U.S. participants.

H3b: Trust in government and attitudes towards preventive measures would be more strongly related to all outcomes (more COVID-19 compliance behavior, less life satisfaction, and more depressive symptoms) in Chinese participants than in U.S. participants.

H3c: The mediation relationship of trust in government and attitude between NFC and compliance behavior, life satisfaction, and depressive symptoms would be more salient in Chinese participants than in U.S. participants.

## Current study

In summary, we sought to examine how NFC, trust in government, and attitudes toward preventive measures predicted COVID-19 compliance behavior and mental health outcomes (depressive symptoms and life satisfaction), whether trust in government and attitudes mediated these relations, and whether there were cultural differences. Specifically, we hypothesized that (a) NFC would be associated with a higher level of trust in government, more positive attitudes towards preventive measures, increased COVID-19 compliance behavior, less life satisfaction, and more depression (H1); (b) trust in government and attitudes towards preventive measures would both mediate the relations between NFC and COVID-19 compliance behavior and mental health outcomes (H2a, H2b, Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#Fig1)); and (c) there would be cultural differences in the mean levels and associations among the above-mentioned variables between the U.S. and Chinese participants (H3a, H3b, H3c).

**Fig. 1**

![Image 7: Fig. 1](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs12144-022-03327-0/MediaObjects/12144_2022_3327_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0/figures/1)

_Hypothesized Model Linking NFC to Compliance Behavior, Depression, and Life Satisfaction via Trust towards Government and Attitudes_

## Method

### Procedures

This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board. We collected data from 346 college students in two large universities located in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States as well as 399 college students from 23 universities in China between March 27 and April 14, 2020. We distributed survey links to college students through university listserv at four universities where most of the participants attended. Researchers also posted the Chinese survey links on social media and recruited an additional 45 students from 21 universities in China.

We invited students to complete an online anonymous survey to share their experiences during COVID-19. Student participation in the survey was voluntary. The U.S. participants received $5 and the participants in China received ¥10 as compensation for their time. The participating U.S. universities had experienced campus closures beginning March 13, 2020, and all universities in China had been closed since February 2020 due to COVID-19.

### Participants

A total of 346 U.S. students completed the survey (68.2% female, _M_ _age_ = 20.48, _SD_ _age_ = 2.30). The sample was diverse in terms of ethnic and racial background, with a majority of the sample being Asian American (48.8%), followed by White (21.4%), African American (15.3%), Latinx (12.1%), and other (2.4%). While a majority of the participants were in the Southeast United States (84.8%), others were in the Northeast (12%), West (0.3%), Midwest (0.3%), and Southwest (0.8%). A total of 399 Chinese students (57.9% female, _M_ _age_ = 21.17, _SD_ _age_ = 2.33) completed the measures included in the current study. While a majority of the participants were in eastern China (68.2%), others were in central China (13.5%) and western China (15.3%).

## Measures

### Demographic information

We collected demographic information, including participants’ age, grade level, gender, and race/ethnicity.

### Need for closure

We used the Need for Closure Scale (Roets & Van Hiel, [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR38 "Roets, A., & Van Hiel, A. (2011). Item selection and validation of a brief, 15-item version of the Need for Closure Scale. Personality and Individual Differences, 50(1), 90–94. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2010.09.004
                  
                ")) to measure NFC. Participants rated 15 items on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = _strongly disagree_, 6 = _strongly agree_). In the original study (Roets & Van Hiel, [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR38 "Roets, A., & Van Hiel, A. (2011). Item selection and validation of a brief, 15-item version of the Need for Closure Scale. Personality and Individual Differences, 50(1), 90–94. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2010.09.004
                  
                ")), the internal consistency was high (Cronbach’s α = 0.87) and the convergent and discriminant validity were supported. NFC significantly correlated with right-wing authoritarianism and neuroticism but did not correlate with agreeableness and extraversion (Roets & Van Hiel, [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR38 "Roets, A., & Van Hiel, A. (2011). Item selection and validation of a brief, 15-item version of the Need for Closure Scale. Personality and Individual Differences, 50(1), 90–94. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2010.09.004
                  
                ")). In the present study, confirmatory factory analysis (CFA) suggested that the one-dimension model fit the data well, \(\chi 2\)(75) = 293.205, _p_< .001, AIC = 383.205, CFI = 0.929, RMSEA = 0.063, 90% CI [0.055, 0.070], SRMR = 0.044. The internal consistency reliability was good (_α_ = 0.83).

### Trust in government

We developed a three-item Likert scale in which participants reported to what extent they trusted the government (1 = _strongly disagree_, 6 = _strongly agree_). A sample item was, “I trust that the (federal) government can make the right decision and policy about COVID-19.” The CFA model was saturated (χ 2 (0) = 0, AIC = 12.000, CFI = 1.000), and all three items had loadings higher than 0.90. For the current study, internal consistency reliability was high (_α_ = 0.97). To examine its convergent validity and discriminant validity, we also calculated the correlations between the trust in government scores with the conformity to rules and hedonism subscales in the Portrait Values Questionnaire (Schwartz et al., [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR39 "Schwartz, S. H., Cieciuch, J., Vecchione, M., Davidov, E., Fischer, R., Beierlein, C., Ramos, A., Verkasalo, M., Lönnqvist, J.-E., Demirutku, K., Dirilen-Gumus, O., & Konty, M. (2012). Refining the theory of basic individual values. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(4), 663–688. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029393
                  
                ")). Trust in government significantly correlated with conformity to rules, _r_ = .333, _p_< .001, but not with hedonism, _r_ = .01, _p_ = .81. The correlations were consistent with the theory because when people trust the government, they are more likely to value conformity to rules. Trust in government was not theoretically related to hedonism. Participants’ scores on trust in government were also consistent with their qualitative answers to the question, “How did COVID-19 change your view of life?” (see the qualitative [results](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#Sec20) section).

### Attitudes towards pandemic preventive measures

Participants were asked to report to what extent they agreed (1 = _strongly disagree_, 6 = _strongly agree_) with the following statements: “I think maintaining social distance (e.g., remaining at home) to contain the virus is a behavior that benefits me,” and “I think wearing a facial mask (if available) during COVID-19 is a behavior that benefits me.” For the current study, the correlation between the two items was significant (_r_ = .537, _p_< .001). Regarding convergent validity, attitudes was significantly correlated with pandemic compliance behavior, _r_ = .41, _p_< .001, as well as trust in government, _r_ = .43, _p_< .001, and conformity to rules in the Portrait Values Questionnaire, _r_ = .28, _p_< .001. Regarding discriminant validity, attitudes was not correlated with the hedonism subscales in the Portrait Values Questionnaire (Schwartz et al., [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR39 "Schwartz, S. H., Cieciuch, J., Vecchione, M., Davidov, E., Fischer, R., Beierlein, C., Ramos, A., Verkasalo, M., Lönnqvist, J.-E., Demirutku, K., Dirilen-Gumus, O., & Konty, M. (2012). Refining the theory of basic individual values. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(4), 663–688. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029393
                  
                ")), r = .02, _p = ._ 51.

### Pandemic compliance behaviors

We developed two items to assess compliance with COVID-19 prevention guidelines. The two items were: “I am complying with the rules and regulations from the health care system (e.g., social distancing, shelter in place) to try to contain the virus” and “I found it easy to comply with the rules and regulations of the health care system to try to contain the virus.” A 6-point response scale (1 = _strongly disagree_, 6 = _strongly agree_) was used. The correlation between the two items was significant (_r_ = .377, _p_< .001). Regarding convergent validity, pandemic compliance behavior was significantly correlated with attitudes towards pandemic preventive behavior, _r_ = .41, _p_< .001, and the conformity to rules subscale in the Portrait Values Questionnaire (Schwartz et al., [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR39 "Schwartz, S. H., Cieciuch, J., Vecchione, M., Davidov, E., Fischer, R., Beierlein, C., Ramos, A., Verkasalo, M., Lönnqvist, J.-E., Demirutku, K., Dirilen-Gumus, O., & Konty, M. (2012). Refining the theory of basic individual values. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(4), 663–688. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029393
                  
                ")), r = .381, _p_< .001. Regarding discriminant validity, pandemic behavior was not related to power dominance in the Portrait Values Questionnaire, _r_ = − .03, _p_ = .39.

### Depression symptoms

To assess depression symptoms experienced during the past 2 weeks, we used the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9; Kroenke et al., [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR26 "Kroenke, K., Spitzer, R. L., & Williams, J. B. (2001). The PHQ-9: Validity of a brief depression severity measure. Journal of General Internal Medicine, 16(9), 606–613. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1525-1497.2001.016009606.x
                  
                ")). All 9 items are rated on a 4-point scale (0 = _not at all_, 1 = _several days_, 2 = _more than half the days_, 3 = _nearly every day_). The PHQ-9 is a commonly used measure for depression, and a sufficient number of prior studies have demonstrated good reliability and validity of the PHQ-9 (e.g., Kroenke et al., [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR27 "Kroenke, K., Spitzer, R., Williams, J., & Löwe, B. (2010). The Patient Health Questionnaire Somatic, Anxiety, and Depressive Symptom Scales: A systematic review. General Hospital Psychiatry, 32(4), 345–359. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2010.03.006
                  
                ")). In the present study, CFA results showed that the model fit well, χ 2 (23) = 117.160, _p_< .001, AIC = 161.160, CFI = 0.971, RMSEA = 0.074, 90% CI [0.061, 0.088], SRMR = 0.031. The internal consistency reliability was good (_α_ = 0.90).

### Life satisfaction

Life Satisfaction, as a component of subjective well-being, is defined “as a summary assessment of a person’s quality of life based on her or his own unique expectations, values, and previous experiences” (Zeng et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR43 "Zeng, Y., Ling, Y., Huebner, E. S., He, Y., & Fu, P. (2018). Assessing the measurement invariance of the Brief Multidimensional Students’ Life Satisfaction Scale in Chinese and American adolescents. Quality of Life Research, 27(1), 259–266. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11136-017-1688-0
                  
                "), p.259). To measure participants’ life satisfaction, we used the Student’s Life Satisfaction Scale (SLSS; Huebner [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR24 "Huebner, E. S. (1991). Initial development of the Student’s Life Satisfaction Scale. School Psychology International, 12(3), 231–240. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0143034391123010
                  
                ")), which measures a global evaluation of an individual’s quality of life that goes beyond the judgment of specific life domains. In our study, we asked participants to evaluate their quality of life as a whole. Sample items were “My life is going well” and “I have what I want in life.” The items in the scale were not modified to reflect changes related to the COVID-19 pandemic as the items were intended to be a general evaluation of life. Participants rated seven items on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = _strongly disagree_, 6 = _strongly agree_). The SLSS has demonstrated respectable psychometric properties (e.g., high test-retest and internal consistency reliability, and significant relationships with other measures of life satisfaction; Gilman & Huebner [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR18 "Gilman, R., & Huebner, E. S. (1997). Children’s reports of their life satisfaction: Convergence across raters, time and response formats. School Psychology International, 18(3), 229–243. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0143034397183004
                  
                ")). In the present study, CFA results showed that the revised model fit well, χ 2 (7) = 39.664, _p_< .001, AIC = 67.664, CFI = 0.978, RMSEA = 0.079, 90% CI [0.056, 0.104], SRMR = 0.033. The internal consistency reliability of the revised SLSS was acceptable (_α_ = 0.79).

### Quantitative data analysis

We used Amos to examine the relation between variables of interest. We conducted CFA to examine the factor structure of the whole measurement model with all the items. CFA results showed that the model fit well, χ 2 (665) = 1977.000, _p_< .001, AIC = 2207.000, CFI = 0.900, RMSEA = 0.051, 90% CI [0.049, 0.054], SRMR = 0.067. Next, we ran SEM to examine the relationship among latent constructs. To examine the mediation model, we used bootstrapping analysis (_n_ = 2,000) to examine the indirect effects because this method has adequate control of Type I errors (Preacher & Hayes, [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-022-03327-0#ref-CR37 "Preacher, K. J., & Hayes, A. F. (2008). Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models. Behavior Research Methods, 40, 879–891")). We considered that a significant indirect effect was observed if the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the indirect effect did not contain a zero.

### Qualitative data

Participants rated whether or not they agreed with the statement, “COVID-19 has changed my view of life,” and then were asked to explain how COVID-19 changed their view of life. args.summary:
This academic article published in Current Psychology (2022) examines how Need for Cognitive Closure (NFC) and trust in government predicted COVID-19 pandemic compliance behaviors and mental health outcomes among college students in the United States and China. The study surveyed 745 college students (399 from China, 346 from the U.S.) between March 27 and April 14, 2020.

Key findings:
- Chinese participants trusted their government more, believed COVID preventive measures were more beneficial, reported more pandemic compliance, and had fewer depressive symptoms than U.S. participants.
- Trust in government and attitudes toward preventive measures mediated the relationship between NFC and pandemic compliance behaviors among Chinese participants, but not U.S. participants.
- NFC predicted better mental health outcomes among Chinese participants compared to U.S. participants.
- Trust in government mediated NFC and mental health outcomes among Chinese participants.
- Trust in government predicted better mental health (fewer depressive symptoms and more life satisfaction) in both countries.

Theoretical frameworks used include uncertainty reduction theory, NFC framework, theory of reasoned action, and individualism-collectivism framework. The study used validated measures including the Need for Closure Scale (15-item), PHQ-9 for depression, Student's Life Satisfaction Scale, and researcher-developed measures for trust in government, attitudes toward preventive measures, and pandemic compliance behaviors.

The U.S. sample was 68.2% female (mean age 20.48), diverse in ethnicity (48.8% Asian American, 21.4% White, 15.3% African American, 12.1% Latinx). The Chinese sample was 57.9% female (mean age 21.17), mostly from eastern China (68.2%).

### Definition

Need for cognitive closure refers to the desire or motivation to have a definite answer or knowledge instead of uncertainty or doubt. The need for closure is resolved by any answer, and the answer is accepted simply because it is available. Thus, need for closure does not refer to knowledge or decisions regarding a specific question, nor does it refer to the need for accuracy. The need for closure can arise from within the person, as a personality trait—or from the situation, such as when it is urgent to make a decision quickly.

### History and Modern Usage

Early psychologists used ideas similar to need for closure, such as openness to experience and intolerance of ambiguity, to refer to broad personality traits and an often dysfunctional style of thinking. Today, need for closure is described as a broader motivation that may affect how a person thinks or reacts in a situation. In addition, need for closure is described as both a stable personality trait and as something that can be provoked by the situation.

Situations that may trigger need for closure include those in which failing to decide has harmful consequences, as well as situations in which the act of thinking about or working on the task is unpleasant. For example, pressure to make quick decisions, boring tasks, and uncomfortable environments (e.g., extreme heat or noise) tend to increase need for closure. In contrast, individuals may avoid closure when the task is enjoyable or the answer is obviously wrong. In addition, individuals vary in their need for closure. Across situations, some individuals prefer to have firm answers quickly, whereas others are more comfortable with uncertainty.

One consequence of need for closure is urgency, or the desire to come to an answer quickly. Urgency leads to a tendency to quickly seize upon the first information that provides an answer. A second consequence of need for closure is permanence, or the tendency to stick to an answer. Permanence leads to a tendency to freeze upon the answer or decision once it is reached. Thus, need for closure may lead individuals to focus only on the initial information provided and to be less likely to change their answers when confronted with new evidence.

The urgency and permanence tendencies of need for closure have been shown to affect how individuals consider information. Need for closure results in focusing on initial information when forming impressions of others, searching for fewer alternative explanations, and using more stereotypes. Need for closure may result in less empathy and perspective taking because these may challenge one's own judgment. Need for closure may also result in being less persuaded by other people's arguments and a preference to interact with people who are more susceptible to persuasion. During group interaction, need for closure may also result in less tolerance of group members who disagree with the majority or who may hinder task completion.

args.summary:
The webpage is an entry from the Encyclopedia of Social Psychology, edited by Roy F. Baumeister and Kathleen D. Vohs, defining and explaining the concept of "Need for Closure." 

**Definition:** Need for cognitive closure refers to the desire or motivation to have a definite answer or knowledge instead of uncertainty or doubt. It is resolved by any available answer and does not refer to the need for accuracy. It can arise from within the person as a personality trait or from the situation.

**History and Modern Usage:** Early psychologists used related concepts like openness to experience and intolerance of ambiguity. Today, need for closure is described as both a stable personality trait and something that can be provoked by situations.

**Triggers:** Situations that may trigger need for closure include those where failing to decide has harmful consequences, or when thinking about the task is unpleasant (e.g., pressure to make quick decisions, boring tasks, uncomfortable environments like extreme heat or noise). Individuals may avoid closure when the task is enjoyable or the answer is obviously wrong.

**Consequences:** Two main consequences are identified: (1) Urgency — the desire to come to an answer quickly, leading to seizing upon the first information that provides an answer; and (2) Permanence — the tendency to stick to an answer once reached, leading to freezing upon a decision. Need for closure can lead to focusing on initial information, searching for fewer alternative explanations, using more stereotypes, less empathy and perspective-taking, being less persuaded by others' arguments, and preferring to interact with people who are more susceptible to persuasion. In groups, it results in less tolerance of members who disagree with the majority.

**Authors:** Janice R. Kelly and Jennifer R. Spoor.

<webpage_content>
Persuasive Patterns: [Influence](/playbooks/influence)

# Need for Closure

We have a desire for definite cognitive closure as opposed to enduring ambiguity

![Illustration of Need for Closure](/uploads/plays/persuasive-pattern/need-for-closure.png)

Run a Need for Closure play

The “Need for Closure” refers to an individual’s desire for a definitive answer or clarity on a subject, as opposed to ambiguity or uncertainty.

Imagine someone who has been working on a project for weeks. They’ve invested a lot of time and effort into it, and they’re close to finishing. However, they receive feedback suggesting that there might be a better approach. Instead of considering the new approach, they feel compelled to continue with their current path, even if it might not yield the best results. Their need for closure, the desire to have a definitive answer and avoid ambiguity, drives them to stick with their initial plan, even when presented with potentially better alternatives.

Now, consider a user who starts signing up for an online service. Halfway through the registration process, they realize that another platform might offer better features. However, the sign-up process on the current platform indicates that they’re “70% complete.” This progress bar, indicating how close they are to completion, taps into their need for closure. Instead of abandoning the process and starting over on a potentially better platform, they feel compelled to finish what they’ve started, driven by the desire to achieve that 100% completion.

> **Our need for closure impacts decision-making**
>
> In the mid-1990s, researchers Arie Kruglanski and Donna Webster embarked on a series of experiments to dive deeper into the cognitive motivations behind the human desire for conclusive answers.
>
> In one of their notable experiments, participants were presented with ambiguous situations and were measured on their urgency to resolve them. Some participants were found to have a high need for closure, wanting immediate and definitive answers, while others were more at ease with the ambiguity, willing to explore various possibilities before arriving at a conclusion. This urgency in the high need for closure group wasn’t just a mere preference; it impacted their decision-making process, often leading them to seize on details that would provide quick answers and “freeze” on that information, ignoring subsequent details that might challenge their conclusions. This phenomenon was termed the “Need for Closure,” highlighting a fundamental cognitive difference in how individuals approach uncertainty and decision-making.
>
> Kruglanski, A. W., & Webster, D. M. (1996). Motivated closing of the mind: “Seizing” and “freezing.” Psychological Review, 103(2), 263-283.

The Need for Closure is a cognitive pattern where individuals seek resolution or clarity, especially in situations that are ambiguous or open-ended. This need can drive people to make decisions more quickly, favoring a clear path or solution rather than lingering in a state of uncertainty. In product design and marketing, understanding this pattern can help in creating experiences that provide clear answers, streamline decision-making processes, or offer resolutions that satisfy this innate psychological need.

The Need for Closure is fundamentally rooted in the human desire for predictability and the discomfort of ambiguity. It is a motivational principle where individuals seek a firm answer to a question and an aversion to uncertainty.

> **Sidestepping decisions by relying on other biases**
>
> Otto, Clarkson, and Kardes (2016) examined the concept of “decision sidestepping.” Their research aimed to uncover the strategies individuals employ when they have a strong motivation for closure. The study revealed that those with a high need for closure tend to sidestep the decision-making process by relying on strategies such as default bias, choice delegation, status quo bias, inaction inertia, and option fixation. These strategies are essentially shortcuts, allowing individuals to reduce the mental effort associated with decision-making. The underlying reason? To ease future decisions and minimize the discomfort of uncertainty. This study provides valuable insights into how the need for closure can influence not just the decisions we make, but also the way we approach decision-making itself.
>
> Otto, A. S., Clarkson, J., & Kardes, F. (2016). Decision sidestepping: How the motivation for closure prompts individuals to bypass decision making. Journal of personality and social psychology, 111(1), 1-16.

Historically, the concept of the need for closure can trace its origins to early psychological theories around discomfort with ambiguity. However, it was in the 1990s, with the work of Kruglanski and Webster, that the term “Need for Closure” was formally introduced and became a focal point of study in cognitive and social psychology.

In their 1996 paper, Kruglanski and Webster identified two primary processes within the need for closure: “seizing” and “freezing.”

* **Seizing**   
   Grabbing onto information quickly to form a judgment or decision. An individual with a high need for closure might seize on the first piece of information they come across to form an opinion.
* **Freezing**   
   Once an opinion or decision is formed, there’s a tendency to “freeze” on it, meaning they become closed off to subsequent information that might challenge or change that decision.

Individuals with a high need for closure tend to make decisions more quickly. They often favor clear, immediate answers over spending time deliberating multiple options or dealing with uncertainty. This urgency isn’t just a preference; it impacts their entire decision-making process. They might seize early on details that provide quick answers and then “freeze” on that information, ignoring subsequent details that might challenge their initial conclusions.

A heightened need for closure leads to an aversion to ambiguous situations. People might avoid situations, tasks, or decisions that present too many unknowns or that might not have a clear, immediate resolution.

In situations where feedback suggests an alternative approach or introduces elements of doubt, those with a high need for closure might resist the new information, preferring to stick to their current path to achieve a sense of completion faster.

## Designing products with the Need for Closure

At the core of this pattern is the innate human compulsion to achieve completeness. Whether it’s filling out a profile, achieving a set goal, or watching a series of short videos, the drive to complete tasks can be harnessed to guide user behavior. For instance, platforms can prompt users by highlighting what’s left undone, subtly nudging them toward completion. But beyond just indicating incompletion, it’s also crucial to delineate a clear, straightforward path toward achieving that closure. The easier and more intuitive the path, the more likely users will be to follow through.

Ensure that your design process considers the user’s journey from start to finish. Every touchpoint should lead them closer to a sense of completion.

Simple, direct instructions and immediate feedback mechanisms can reassure users that they’re on the right track. Onboarding processes, for instance, benefit immensely from this understanding. Instead of overwhelming users with numerous options or excessive information, a streamlined, step-by-step walkthrough can help them quickly grasp the product’s core functionalities, satisfying their need for closure.

Give users something to strive for. Whether it’s profile completion on a social platform or a multi-stage checkout process in an e-commerce app, clear milestones guide users. It gives them a roadmap of what’s achieved and what remains. This not only makes the journey intuitive but also gives users a sense of progress, compelling them to see tasks through to completion.

Much like milestones, progress indicators, be it in the form of bars, percentages, or checklists, can be a powerful tool. They visually represent the user’s journey, subtly nudging them towards completion. For instance, multi-step forms with progress bars can reduce abandonment rates as users, having invested time in filling prior sections, are less likely to drop off midway.

Rather than merely focusing on what’s done, sometimes it’s essential to highlight what’s left. Platforms can use subtle cues like notifications or visual markers to indicate incomplete tasks. This plays on the user’s aversion to incompletion, driving them to act.

Identifying incompletion is half the battle. The other half is providing users with a clear, straightforward path to resolution. Making this path intuitive, with minimal steps, can significantly increase the likelihood of task completion. For instance, if a user hasn’t filled out a particular section of their profile, a direct link to that section can guide them to act.

Humans are driven not just by the need to complete but also by rewards. Consider introducing incentives for task completion. This could range from badges in a gamified environment, discounts in e-commerce platforms, or even access to exclusive content. The prospect of a reward, combined with the desire for closure, can be a potent mix.

To tap into our Need for Closure, the path to completion needs to be clear and straightforward. Closure should be attainable and decisions should be easy. While offering choices empowers users, there are moments in the user journey where too many options can be counterproductive – especially when tapping into our innate Need for Closure. Particularly at critical junctures, like finalizing a purchase, minimizing choices can reduce indecision and promote action.

One tactic playing on our need for closure is giving users a head start, artificially advancing their progress. Instead of giving a blank stamp card, offer one with a couple of stamps already on it. This initial advancement can drive users to complete the card, given they perceive they are already partway through.

## Ethical recommendations

This pattern can, like many others, be manipulated in ways that are not in the user’s best interest.

* **Endless loops**   
   Some platforms, knowing the human desire for closure, may create never-ending tasks or loops, keeping users engaged far longer than they intended. This could lead to excessive screen time, distraction from important tasks, or even financial costs.
* **Artificial scarcity**   
   By creating a perception that an opportunity is fleeting or a task must be completed immediately, users might be pushed into making hasty decisions they later regret. For instance, an online shopping platform might use limited-time offers or countdown timers to push sales, exploiting the need for closure to urge a purchase.
* **Information overload**   
   The need for closure might be used to encourage users to provide excessive personal data, under the guise of “completing a profile” or “finishing a survey,” leading to potential privacy concerns.

To ensure that your application of the Need for Closure pattern, use these rules of thumbs as a checklist as you design with the pattern in mind.

* **User control**   
   Give users the ability to pause, save progress, or opt-out of tasks, especially those that are long or recurring. This respects their autonomy and decision-making.
* **Avoid artificial urgency**   
   While it’s acceptable to highlight the benefits of completing a task, avoid creating undue pressure or urgency that might lead users to make decisions they haven’t fully considered.
* **Privacy first**   
   If collecting user data, always explain why it’s needed and how it will be used. Ensure that any data collection is compliant with privacy laws and best practices.

## Real life Need for Closure examples

### LinkedIn

When users have an incomplete profile, LinkedIn notifies them, often stating, “You’re just a few steps away from completing your profile.” By doing this, they not only highlight the incompleteness but also provide a clear roadmap for users to achieve closure. Furthermore, they offer rewards for profile completion, further motivating users.

### Fitbit

Fitbit sets daily goals for steps, active minutes, and floors climbed. The dashboard displays how close or far a user is from achieving these goals. The visual representation of daily progress encourages users to complete their fitness goals, promoting consistent physical activity throughout the day.

### Netflix

When watching a series on Netflix, the next episode starts automatically with a brief countdown, playing on the viewer’s need for closure to finish the series or at least watch the next episode. This feature increases viewing durations as users often opt to continue watching, seeking closure for the storyline.

### Trigger Questions

* How can I visually represent progress or the state of completion to guide users towards achieving closure?
* In what areas can I reduce ambiguity to accelerate decision-making while still offering valuable choices?
* Are there areas in the user journey where simplifying tasks or reducing steps can satisfy the user's need for closure more efficiently?
* How can I provide immediate, clear feedback to users, ensuring they feel they're on the right track towards completion?
* How can I ensure I'm not overwhelming users with excessive information or options, thus hindering their need for closure?
* In what ways might we be inadvertently prolonging a user's journey, denying them a timely sense of closure?
* How can we balance the need for quick closure with the necessity of providing depth and detail?
* Are there areas in our design where users might feel 'stuck' or uncertain, and how can we address this?

Experiences are largely remembered by their peaks and endings. Designing with the Need for Closure in mind ensures that the “endings” of user experiences are satisfactory and memorable, enhancing the overall perception of the product or service. Ensure that the ending moments of any interaction, purchase, or engagement are positive and memorable.

People who have begun a task seek to complete it to attain closure. This aligns with the commitment principle where once a user commits to something (like starting a task), they are more likely to see it through. --- SOURCE 1: When need for closure leads to positive attitudes towards a negatively stereotyped outgroup ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4287659

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article from Motivation and Emotion (2014) investigates the relationship between the need for closure (NFC) and positive attitudes towards a negatively stereotyped outgroup (Gypsies in Poland). The researchers propose that NFC can lead to positive attitudes when accompanied by a low ability to achieve closure (AAC). 

In Study 1 (519 participants, online survey), NFC and AAC were measured as individual characteristics. Results showed that among low AAC individuals, higher NFC was positively associated with positive attitudes and perceived closeness toward Gypsies, while among high AAC individuals, NFC was related to increased negative stereotyping.

In Study 2 (54 students, experimental), AAC was manipulated via informational helplessness training. Results confirmed that participants in the low AAC condition showed a positive relationship between NFC and positive attitudes toward Gypsies, while no significant relationship was found in the control group.

The authors argue that low AAC impairs the ability to construct and apply schemas (like negative stereotypes), causing individuals with high NFC to process more information systematically and develop more balanced or positive evaluations of negatively stereotyped groups. The study extends lay epistemic theory by demonstrating that achieving closure requires specific ability (AAC) and is not merely automatic.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The study examined the relationship between epistemic motivation, which is the need for closure (NFC), and positive attitudes towards a negatively stereotyped outgroup (i.e., Gypsies)., Our results demonstrated that the relationship between positive attitudes and NFC was influenced by AAC, when it was measured as an individual characteristic., In Study 2, we demonstrated that NFC is related to positive attitudes toward Gypsies among people with a decreased sense of personal control (i.e., low AAC condition) compared to a control group without a decreased sense of personal control., One of the implicit assumptions of the lay epistemic theory is that because the cognitive processes associated with high NFC are relatively effortless and automatic, achieving closure is an easy default option, which is available regardless of an individual's ability to carry it through. However, our results provide evidence for the idea that the construction and application of cognitive schemas is not relatively automatic and effort-free., Our findings suggest that inclusion of the concept of AAC as an inherent component of the widely accepted theory of lay epistemology may elucidate our understanding of the process of knowledge formation and use.
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://ojs.tnkul.pl/index.php/rpsych/article/view/615

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Roczniki Psychologiczne (Annals of Psychology) in 2016, presents a review of research on the "need for closure" (NFC) in the context of lay epistemic theory. The authors—Paweł Strojny, Małgorzata Kossowska, and Agnieszka Strojny from Jagiellonian University—explore how NFC, which typically drives simplified and accelerated information processing, can under certain circumstances actually promote complex cognition. The paper focuses on two key theoretical postulates: the two phases of the epistemic process (seizing and freezing) and the dual nature of the need for cognitive closure. While high NFC is often associated with heuristic, simplified processing, the review presents evidence that the typical relationship can be reversed, leading to more elaborate cognitive strategies depending on contextual factors. The article is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Lay epistemic theory is one of the most popular theoretical frameworks describing the knowledge formation process. According to it, the central variable determining the epistemic process is the need for cognitive closure. In most cases, high levels of this motivation are associated with simplified and accelerated processing of information. This can lead to an overly simplified understanding of this variable. In fact, there are reasons to believe that the typical relationship is reversed under certain circumstances.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an adaptation of the Need for Closure Scale (NFC), a 15-question self-assessment measuring an individual's desire for certainty and aversion to ambiguity. The assessment covers five dimensions: Order, Predictability, Ambiguity, Decisiveness, and Closed-mindedness. Scores range from 15-90, with Low NFC (15-30) indicating comfort with ambiguity, Moderate NFC (31-74) reflecting balance, and High NFC (75-90) showing a strong preference for clear answers and structure.

The research behind NFC was introduced by Arie Kruglanski in 1989, with the first validated 42-item scale published by Webster and Kruglanski in 1994. Key mechanisms include 'seizing' (latching onto first available answers) and 'freezing' (resisting new information). The scale evolved through critiques (Neuberg et al., 1997) and revisions (Roets & Van Hiel, 2007, 2011), resulting in a 15-item short form. The assessment uses a 6-point scale with no neutral midpoint, includes 4 reverse-scored items to reduce acquiescence bias, and normalizes facet scores as percentages for comparability.

NFC is both a personal trait and a situational tendency—it rises under time pressure, mental fatigue, and environmental noise. In groups, high-NFC members tend to push for consensus and resist reopening decisions. The tool is intended for educational and self-reflection purposes only, not clinical diagnosis.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

The NFC concept, introduced by Kruglanski (1990), refers to the desire for "an answer on a given topic, any answer… compared to confusion and ambiguity." The original 42-item NFC scale (Webster & Kruglanski, 1994) includes five facet scales: preference for order, preference for predictability, decisiveness, discomfort with ambiguity, and closed-mindedness. A revised 41-item version was later provided by Roets & Van Hiel (2007) to address issues with the decisiveness items.

The 15-item version demonstrated similar psychometric properties and correlations with third variables as the full 41-item revised scale. The brief NFC scale provides researchers with a validated tool for assessing the NFC construct when practical considerations prohibit using the full scale. SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM) of persuasion, developed by psychologist Shelly Chaiken in 1980, is a dual-process theory explaining how people process persuasive messages through two cognitive routes. The heuristic route involves fast, cue-driven judgments using mental shortcuts like the expert heuristic, consensus heuristic, and message length heuristic. The systematic route involves deliberate, content-based analysis requiring motivation and ability. The sufficiency principle explains that people seek the minimum cognitive effort needed to reach acceptable confidence levels. Unlike the similar Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), HSM explicitly allows both routes to operate simultaneously, either additively or with bias. Systematic processing produces more durable, resistant attitude change than heuristic processing. The model has applications in advertising, health communication, political communication, and digital environments. Criticisms include conceptual overlap with ELM, measurement challenges, and underemphasis on emotional factors. The HSM remains a foundational and empirically well-supported model in persuasion research.
</summary>

This Sage Knowledge entry defines the dual-processing model of persuasion, a theory identifying two basic routes to persuasion. The two best-known variants are the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) by Richard Petty and John Cacioppo (1986) and the Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM) by Shelly Chaiken and Alice Eagly (1980/1987). The ELM proposes two primary paths operating in tandem: the central route, which involves high elaboration (in-depth cognitive processing of argument rationality and evidence), and the peripheral route, which relies on tangential cues unrelated to the substantive message. Whether a person engages in central or peripheral processing depends on motivation (topic involvement) and ability (capacity to understand concepts). The entry illustrates these routes through a car-buying example: buyers focused on financing take the central route, while those swayed by imagery and style take the peripheral route. --- SOURCE 13: Heuristic-systematic model of information processing - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heuristic-systematic_model_of_information_processing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The heuristic-systematic model of information processing (HSM) is a dual-process theory of persuasion developed by Shelly Chaiken. It explains how people process persuasive messages through two modes: heuristic processing (using simple decision rules or mental shortcuts with minimal cognitive effort) and systematic processing (careful, deliberative, and comprehensive analysis of message content). The model is grounded in the sufficiency principle and the principle of least effort, suggesting individuals tend to minimize cognitive resource use. HSM is closely related to the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), with heuristic processing analogous to peripheral route processing and systematic processing to central route processing, though HSM specifically focuses on validity-seeking persuasion contexts.

Key aspects include: heuristic processing relies on availability, accessibility, and applicability of stored knowledge structures; systematic processing involves in-depth evaluation of message content and source reliability. The model predicts that attitudes formed through heuristic processing are less stable, less resistant to counterarguments, and less predictive of behavior than those formed through systematic processing. Both processing modes can occur independently or simultaneously.

The model was expanded to include defense-motivation and impression-motivation as additional processing motives beyond accuracy-seeking. Practical applications include advertising, website credibility evaluation, and medical decision-making (e.g., prostate cancer treatment decisions). Criticisms focus on HSM's similarity to ELM and its limitations in defining specific persuasion motivations.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: The Relationship between the Need for Closure and Coronavirus Fear: The Mediating Effect of Beliefs in Conspiracy Theories about COVID-19 ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/19/22/14789

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article titled "The Relationship between the Need for Closure and Coronavirus Fear: The Mediating Effect of Beliefs in Conspiracy Theories about COVID-19," published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (IJERPH) on November 10, 2022. The study, conducted by Sara Staszak, Julia Maciejowska, Wiktoria Urjasz, Tomasz Misiuro, and Andrzej Cudo from the University of Zielona Góra and The John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin in Poland, investigated the relationships between fear of the coronavirus, belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories, and dimensions of the need for cognitive closure.

**Methodology:** The researchers analyzed results from 380 Polish adults (mean age 33.41, 239 females) who completed online versions of the Fear of COVID-19 Scale, a short version of the Need for Closure Scale, and a newly designed Conspiracy Theories about the Coronavirus Scale. The study was conducted between September and October 2020, during a period of high COVID-19 cases in Poland.

**Key Findings:**
- Belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories fully mediated the relationship between fear of the coronavirus and avoidance of ambiguity, as well as closed-mindedness.
- This suggests that conspiracy beliefs may play a significant role in reducing the level of coronavirus fear in people with high levels of these traits.
- A partial mediation between fear of the coronavirus and the need for predictability was also found.

**Theoretical Background:** The article discusses the need for cognitive closure as an epistemic motivation related to seeking clear, certain knowledge to reduce cognitive uncertainty. People with high need for closure tend to use superficial analysis of information and seek confirmation of existing beliefs. The study posits that conspiracy theories provide simple, understandable explanations for complex phenomena, potentially offering a false sense of security and reducing anxiety about the uncertain COVID-19 situation. The research was grounded in Douglas et al.'s theory linking conspiracy beliefs to epistemic, existential, and social motives.

The article includes extensive literature review on coronavirus fear, conspiracy theories, and the need for cognitive closure dimensions (need for predictability, avoidance of ambiguity, and closed-mindedness), with age included as a covariate.
</summary>

</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Beliefs in conspiracy theories and the need for cognitive closure ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3694217

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published in Frontiers in Psychology (2013) by Patrick J. Leman and Marco Cinnirella, examining the relationship between beliefs in conspiracy theories (BICT), the need for cognitive closure (NFCC), and the evaluation of evidence. The study consists of two experiments.

**Study 1 (N=30)** found no relationship between NFCC and BICT, suggesting both advocates and opponents of conspiracy theories can employ rigid thinking. However, BICT correlated positively with feelings of alienation and negatively with interpersonal trust, consistent with prior research. No correlation was found between belief in real-world conspiracies and attributing a conspiracy to a novel (fictitious) event.

**Study 2 (N=86)** manipulated NFCC (via accountability instructions) and evidence type (pro- or anti-conspiracy). Results showed that evidence strongly influenced attributions: pro-conspiracy evidence increased the likelihood rating of a conspiracy explanation, while anti-conspiracy evidence decreased it. A key interaction emerged: when NFCC was lowered (high accountability), the influence of prior BICT on attributions diminished—both high and low BICT groups made similar likelihood ratings. In contrast, under normal NFCC, those with high BICT rated conspiracies more likely and those with low BICT rated them less likely after reading evidence. The effects of evidence were strong but slightly diminished after a 2-hour delay, while BICT effects appeared more enduring.

The authors conclude that biases in evidence evaluation contribute to conspiracy beliefs, but lowering NFCC (increasing accountability and systematic processing) can reduce the influence of prior beliefs. The findings highlight the importance of both cognitive (NFCC) and social factors (alienation, trust) in conspiracy theory beliefs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An important component of conspiracy theories is how they influence, and are influenced by, the evaluation of potential evidence.", "When NFCC was experimentally lowered the effects of prior beliefs in conspiracy theories diminished.", "Alienation and the associated constructs of powerlessness and anomie have consistently been associated with BICT.", "The present findings point to the importance of individual and social factors in mediating levels of belief in conspiracy theory.", "Lowering NFCC (increasing accountability and hence giving participants a greater motivation to scrutinize the evidence and justify their rating) appeared to cancel out the influence of existing BICT."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Need for cognitive closure, political trust, and belief in conspiracy ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/social-psychology/articles/10.3389/frsps.2024.1447313/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Frontiers in Social Psychology original research article (published January 22, 2025) examining the relationship between need for cognitive closure (NCC), political trust, and belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories. The study, conducted by Alexander Jedinger (GESIS) and Lena Masch (University of Münster), uses data from multiple waves of the representative GESIS Panel in Germany (N = 2,883). NCC and political trust were measured pre-pandemic (2018-2019), while COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs were assessed during the second wave of the pandemic (August-October 2020).

Key findings:
- NCC showed a small but significant positive association with COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs (both at bivariate and adjusted levels).
- Political trust (pre-pandemic) and crisis-specific trust were strongly negatively related to conspiracy beliefs.
- Contrary to the authors' central hypotheses, there was no moderating effect of political trust on the NCC-conspiracy belief relationship.
- The final models accounted for 22-37% of variance in conspiracy beliefs.
- Additional predictors of conspiracy beliefs included: lower education, younger age, living in East Germany, right-wing orientation, lower income, and immigration background.
- Most Germans rejected conspiracy theories: only 6.7% scored in the highest range (6-7 on a 7-point scale), while 52.5% found them very unlikely.

The authors conclude that individual differences in epistemic needs play a relatively marginal role compared to political trust, emphasizing the importance of maintaining institutional trust in democratic societies to combat misinformation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: The efficacy of interventions in reducing belief in conspiracy theories: A systematic review - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10075392

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in PLOS ONE (April 5, 2023) by O'Mahony et al. examining the efficacy of interventions in reducing belief in conspiracy theories. The review analyzed 25 studies (total N=7179) and 48 intervention comparisons. Key findings:

- **Overall effectiveness**: Only about 40% of interventions (21 out of 48) successfully changed conspiracy beliefs, with most showing small effects. However, several interventions were particularly effective.

- **Most effective interventions**: 
  1. **Informational inoculations** (pre-emptive debunking before exposure) showed the largest effects, with fact-based inoculations (d=1.31) and logic-based inoculations (d=0.91) being most effective.
  2. **Educational interventions** - A 3-month pseudoscience class showed large effects (d=1.07).
  3. **Analytical/priming interventions** that fostered critical thinking showed small to medium effects (d=0.3-0.56).

- **Less effective**: Traditional counterarguments and debunking after exposure produced only small effects (d=0.13-0.37). Empathetic counterarguments and ridiculing beliefs were among the least effective.

- **Important caveat**: Inoculation effectiveness was easily counteracted by "metainoculations" (warning participants about the intervention), which rendered them ineffective (d=0.58).

- **Backfiring effects**: Some interventions paradoxically increased conspiracy beliefs, including labeling statements as "conspiracy theories" and certain priming manipulations.

- **Key conclusion**: Pre-emptive interventions (before exposure) are more effective than post-hoc debunking. Fostering analytical thinking and critical thinking skills appears promising. The authors note that conspiracy beliefs may be underpinned by inherent susceptibilities that are not easily refuted with standard counterarguments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We found that while the majority of interventions were ineffective in terms of changing conspiracy beliefs, several interventions were particularly effective. Interventions that fostered an analytical mindset or taught critical thinking skills were found to be the most effective in terms of changing conspiracy beliefs.", "Approximately 60% of studies used some form of measure that examined generalised conspiracy belief and ideation (k = 28), while the rest used measures that assessed belief in specific conspiracy theories (k = 6).", "Overall, 21 (~40%) interventions successfully changed conspiracy beliefs when compared to control, baseline, or neutral groups. However, only a small number of these interventions demonstrated large effect sizes (k = 3).", "Inoculations that identified the factual inaccuracies of conspiracy beliefs were found to be the most effective of all the interventions in the review (d = 1.3).", "Pre-emptively refuting the inaccuracies of conspiracy beliefs was much more effective than traditional counterarguments that were given after participants had encountered conspiracy theories."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Motivated closing of the mind: "seizing" and "freezing" - PubMed ---
URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8637961

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed record for a seminal 1996 review article titled "Motivated closing of the mind: 'seizing' and 'freezing'" by A.W. Kruglanski and D.M. Webster, published in Psychological Review (Vol. 103, No. 2, pp. 263-283). The article presents a theoretical framework centered on the need for (nonspecific) cognitive closure—defined as a desire for definite knowledge on some issue. This need is conceptualized both as a stable individual difference and as a situationally evoked state. The framework identifies two general tendencies: the urgency tendency (inclination to attain closure as soon as possible, i.e., "seizing") and the permanence tendency (inclination to maintain closure for as long as possible, i.e., "freezing"). The theory has implications for social-cognitive phenomena at intrapersonal, interpersonal, and group levels, including impression formation, stereotyping, attribution, persuasion, group decision making, and language use in intergroup contexts. The research was supported by NIH grants (1R01 MH 52578 and KO5 MH 01213) and was conducted at the University of Maryland, College Park.
</summary>

"The need for closure is a desire for definite knowledge on some issue. It represents a dimension of stable individual differences as well as a situationally evocable state.", "The urgency tendency represents an individual's inclination to attain closure as soon as possible, and the permanence tendency represents an individual's inclination to maintain it for as long as possible.", "Empirical evidence for present theory attests to diverse need for closure effects on fundamental social psychological phenomena, including impression formation, stereotyping, attribution, persuasion, group decision making, and language use in intergroup contexts."

--- SOURCE 9: Motivated reasoning - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivated_reasoning

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Motivated Reasoning** is a mental process where individuals access, construct, and evaluate beliefs in response to new information, arriving at desired conclusions due to their biases. While people tend to reach conclusions they want, these desires are constrained by the ability to construct reasonable justifications (Kunda, 1990). The concept is closely related to cognitive dissonance and confirmation bias, serving as a mechanism to relieve psychological stress from contradictory beliefs.

**Two Categories:**
1. **Accuracy-oriented (non-directional):** Motive is to arrive at an accurate conclusion. Research shows accuracy goals increase the quantity and quality of cognitive processing, delaying premature conclusions. However, accuracy goals do not always eliminate biases.
2. **Goal-oriented (directional):** Motive is to reach a particular conclusion favored based on identity protection and shared values. This involves biased memory search and belief construction mechanisms.

**Neuroscientific evidence** (Westen et al., 2006) suggests motivated reasoning is qualitatively distinct from cold reasoning, engaging affective processing rather than purely cognitive neural regions. This can create neural pathways that reinforce beliefs over time through "affective contagion."

**Political bias:** A 2018 meta-analysis by Ditto and colleagues found both liberal and conservative political orientations are susceptible to bias to the same extent, though this finding was disputed.

**Examples include:** Smoking (justifying continued tobacco use despite health evidence), COVID-19 (mask/vaccine refusal based on motivated reasoning, with 2024 research showing even vaccinated individuals developed preferences for their assigned vaccine brand), climate change denial, Obama "birther" conspiracy theories, and immigration attitudes shaped by political ideology.

**Information sources:** Social media creates echo chambers where users accept content aligning with their beliefs. News media research shows people over-trust non-credible "fake news" sources that align with their political beliefs. The hostile media effect occurs when individuals reason away small amounts of contrary information, becoming more entrenched in their beliefs over time.
</summary>

Motivated reasoning is a mental process through which individuals access, construct, and evaluate their beliefs in response to new information or experiences where their biases cause them to arrive at desired conclusions., While most people may be more likely to arrive at conclusions they want, such desires are generally constrained by the ability to construct a reasonable justification., Political reasoning involves the goal of identity protection or maintaining status within an affinity group united by shared values., Motivated reasoning was not associated with neural activity in regions previously linked with cold reasoning tasks nor conscious (explicit) emotion regulation., Both political orientations are susceptible to bias to the same extent.

--- SOURCE 10: Need for (Cognitive) Closure Scale (NFCS) ---
URL: https://sjdm.org/dmidi/Need_for_(Cognitive)_Closure_Scale.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage describes the Need for (Cognitive) Closure Scale (NFCS), a psychological assessment tool designed to measure an individual's motivation to seek an answer and end further information processing, even if that answer is not the best or correct one. The scale was developed by Kruglanski, Webster, and Klem (1993) and Webster and Kruglanski (1994). A revised 15-item short version is available from Roets & Van Hiel (2011).

**Key Details:**
- **Purpose:** Assesses "motivation with respect to information processing and judgment" — specifically the desire for an answer to end further processing.
- **Questions:** 42 items rated on a 6-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree).
- **Sub-scales (5):** Desire for predictability, Preference for order and structure, Discomfort with ambiguity, Decisiveness, Close-mindedness.
- **Sample Items:** Include statements about preferring to know what to expect, valuing clear rules, preferring certainty over uncertainty, making decisions quickly, and not consulting many opinions.
- **Related scales:** Personal Need for Structure and Personal Fear of Invalidity (Thompson et al., 2001).
- **References:** Includes original scale development references, usage studies in areas such as anxiety disorders, delusions, closed-mindedness, social judgment, and entrepreneurship, as well as a discussion/debate about the scale's psychometric properties (Kruglanski et al., 1997 vs. Neuberg et al., 1997).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: [PDF] Persuasion by a Single Route: A View from the Unimodel Author(s) ---
URL: https://www.uni-muenster.de/imperia/md/content/psyifp/aeechterhoff/vorlesungkommunikation/kruglanski_thompson_perssingleroute_psychinq1999.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a target article from Psychological Inquiry (1999) by Kruglanski and Thompson proposing a "unimodel" of persuasion as an alternative to the dominant dual-process models (ELM and HSM). The article argues that the central/systematic and peripheral/heuristic routes to persuasion are not qualitatively different processes but rather represent functionally equivalent types of evidence from which persuasive conclusions are drawn via the same underlying syllogistic reasoning process.

The authors first review the two major dual-process models: Petty and Cacioppo's Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), which posits central and peripheral routes, and Chaiken and Eagly's Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM), which posits systematic and heuristic modes. Both models share the assumption of two qualitatively different persuasion modes, with the more extensive mode (central/systematic) depending on sufficient motivation and ability.

The unimodel, based on the Lay Epistemic Theory (LET), reconceptualizes cues and message arguments as different contents of evidence relevant to a conclusion, rather than representing different processes. Evidence is defined as information linked to a conclusion via a prior mental premise (if-then reasoning). Both source cues (e.g., "Dr. Smith is an expert") and message arguments (e.g., "freon destroys the ozone layer") function as minor premises in syllogistic reasoning.

The authors argue that motivation and cognitive capacity affect persuasion uniformly regardless of whether evidence comes from cues or arguments. They discuss various motivations (accuracy, need for closure, need for cognition, directional motivations) and cognitive ability factors (capability/software, capacity/hardware) that impact persuasion.

The article presents the argument that once differences in informational parameters (relevance, complexity, accessibility) are controlled for, cue-based and message argument-based persuasion should be affected similarly by processing variables, challenging the discriminant validity of the dual-process distinction.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Major current notions of persuasion depict it as attainable via 2 qualitatively distinct routes: (a) a central or a systematic route in which opinions and attitudes are based on carefully processed arguments in the persuasive message and (b) a peripheral or heuristic route in which they are based on briefly considered heuristics or cues, exogenous to the message.", "This article offers a single-route reconceptualization that treats these dual routes to persuasion as involving functionally equivalent types of evidence from which persuasive conclusions may be drawn.", "The unimodel (a) adopts a more abstract level of analysis in which the two persuasive modes (of either ELM or HSM) are viewed as special cases of the same underlying process and (b) deconstructs the 'Laswellian' partition between persuasively relevant categories.", "The crucial distinction between cues and/or heuristics on the one hand and message arguments on the other refers to informational contents relevant to a conclusion, rather than to a principled difference in the persuasion process as such.", "According to LET, evidence refers to information relevant to a conclusion. Relevance, in turn, implies a prior linkage between general categories such that affirmation of one in a specific case (observation of the evidence) affects one's belief in the other (e.g., warrants the conclusion)."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Roczniki Psychologiczne (Annals of Psychology) in 2016, presents a review of research on the "need for closure" (NFC) in the context of lay epistemic theory. The authors—Paweł Strojny, Małgorzata Kossowska, and Agnieszka Strojny from Jagiellonian University—explore how NFC, which typically drives simplified and accelerated information processing, can under certain circumstances actually promote complex cognition. The paper focuses on two key theoretical postulates: the two phases of the epistemic process (seizing and freezing) and the dual nature of the need for cognitive closure. While high NFC is often associated with heuristic, simplified processing, the review presents evidence that the typical relationship can be reversed, leading to more elaborate cognitive strategies depending on contextual factors. According to it, the central variable determining the epistemic process is the need for cognitive closure. In most cases, high levels of this motivation are associated with simplified and accelerated processing of information. This can lead to an overly simplified understanding of this variable. In fact, there are reasons to believe that the typical relationship is reversed under certain circumstances.

URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closure_(psychology)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Closure (psychology), also known as need for closure (NFC) or need for cognitive closure (NFCC), is a social psychological term describing an individual's desire for a clear, firm answer or resolution to avoid ambiguity. The concept was developed by Arie Kruglanski and colleagues. It operates through two tendencies: the urgency tendency (attaining closure quickly) and the permanence tendency (maintaining closure). The need for closure is a fairly stable individual characteristic that can be affected by situational factors.

The Need for Closure Scale (NFCS), developed in 1993, is a 42-item instrument measuring this construct. High scorers tend to exhibit primacy effects, correspondence bias, stereotypical judgments, and resistance to persuasion. Low scorers express more creativity. The scale has been revised over time, including a 15-item abridged version. NFC correlates positively with authoritarianism, dogmatism, and conservatism, and negatively with cognitive complexity.

Functionally opposite is the need to avoid closure, reflecting the desire to suspend judgment. Lack of closure leaves situations in ambiguity. High NFC can invite bias in information selection, cognitive manipulation, judgment, and decision-making. It has implications for consumer behavior, prejudice, preference for autocratic influence, and educational processes. Research shows high NFC individuals use more cognitive heuristics, have lower creativity scores, and show bias against deviant stimuli. The concept of "closure" has also been applied in legal contexts, particularly regarding the death penalty.
</summary>

This study investigated the relationship between fear of COVID-19, belief in conspiracy theories, and dimensions of the need for cognitive closure. Key results include: a negative correlation between coronavirus fear and belief in conspiracy theories; a positive correlation between coronavirus fear and avoidance of ambiguity and need for predictability; and a positive correlation between belief in conspiracy theories and age. The model explained 22% of the variance in coronavirus fear. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article from the Annual Review of Developmental Psychology (2024) by Edelson, Reyna, Singh, and Roue (Cornell University) examining the psychology of misinformation across the lifespan. The authors review mechanisms of misinformation susceptibility, why it spreads, and how these operate developmentally, presenting a theoretical framework based on fuzzy-trace theory.

**Key Findings:**

- **Individual Differences:** Cognitive ability, analytical thinking style, numeracy, and metacognitive scrutiny are protective against misinformation. Content knowledge alone is insufficient; gist plausibility (whether something seems true in principle) determines acceptance.
- **Developmental Vulnerabilities:** Children and adolescents are less capable of metacognitive monitoring, have lower cognitive ability, and are less willing to think analytically. Young people and older adults may be at greatest risk due to prioritization of social goals.
- **Knowledge:** Factual knowledge increases with age and education, and is protective. However, "knowledge neglect" occurs when people fail to use knowledge they possess. The Moses illusion exemplifies this.
- **Numeracy:** Only 36% of 4th graders and 26% of 8th graders are proficient in math (2022 NAEP), limiting their ability to interpret numerical misinformation (e.g., VAERS vaccine data).
- **Cognitive Ability:** Higher intelligence is associated with lower belief in fake news, but the mechanisms are complex—involving knowledge, logical reasoning, and gist-based plausibility.
- **Thinking Style:** Actively open-minded thinking (AOT) and Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) performance predict better truth discernment. However, children scoring high on CRT-D still could not translate this into better fake news discrimination without content knowledge.
- **Emotion:** Heightened emotion is associated with worse truth discernment in adults. Adolescents experience more frequent/intense emotions, potentially increasing vulnerability.
- **Motivation & Ideology:** Partisan bias in truth discernment is well-documented; accuracy incentives can reduce it by about 30%. Social consensus strongly influences belief, especially for young people.
- **Personality:** Agreeableness and conscientiousness are protective; neuroticism increases vulnerability. Adverse childhood experiences can create mistrust and susceptibility to conspiracy-themed misinformation.
- **Repetition:** Repetition increases truth ratings (illusory truth effect), but older adults show resistance to this effect for known statements.

**Theoretical Framework (Fuzzy-Trace Theory):** The authors distinguish verbatim truth (precise details) from gist truth (underlying meaning). People often believe misinformation because they believe its gist to be true, even when realizing it's literally false. Misinformation works by conveying a compelling gist interpretation that stirs emotion. Interventions must educate intuition with content knowledge, not just instill critical attitudes.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Personality and Individual Differences (Volume 50, Issue 1, January 2011, Pages 90-94) by Arne Roets and Alain Van Hiel presents the development and validation of a brief 15-item version of the Need for Closure (NFC) Scale. The Need for Closure concept, introduced by Kruglanski (1990), refers to the desire for "an answer on a given topic, any answer… compared to confusion and ambiguity." The original 42-item NFC scale (Webster & Kruglanski, 1994) includes five facet scales: Preference for Order, Preference for Predictability, Decisiveness, Discomfort with Ambiguity, and Closed-mindedness. A revised 41-item version was later developed by Roets & Van Hiel (2007) to address contamination of the Decisiveness items with ability-content rather than motivational need.

Researchers frequently used unvalidated, idiosyncratic abridged versions of the scale, selecting items arbitrarily without reporting or validating their selections. This study aimed to provide an empirically validated short version. Using an aggregated heterogeneous sample (N=1584), the authors analyzed component loadings of the 41 revised NFC items and selected the three highest-loading items from each of the five facet scales, resulting in a 15-item brief NFC scale. Psychometric analyses showed the 15-item version had similar properties to the full 41-item scale and nearly identical correlations with third variables. The brief NFC scale provides researchers with a useful tool for assessing the NFC construct when practical considerations prohibit using the full scale. The article has been cited 492 times according to the metrics shown.

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12891588

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in *Scientific Reports* (2026) by Katarzyna Growiec and Ewa Szumowska, examining the relationship between Need for Cognitive Closure (NFC) and preference for similar others in social networks.

The researchers hypothesized that individuals high in NFC—who are motivated to avoid ambiguity and quickly resolve uncertainty—would prefer homophilous (similar) interactions over heterophilous (dissimilar) ones, because interacting with similar others reduces uncertainty.

**Correlational Studies 1–4:** Across four independent samples (Polish economics students, Polish psychology students, Polish students from various majors, and U.S. students), higher NFC was consistently associated with lower heterophily (fewer interactions with dissimilar others). A meta-analysis confirmed a significant negative association (β = −0.20, p < .001). High-NFC individuals also reported fewer acquaintances and fewer people to discuss important matters with, though NFC was unrelated to number of close family/friends.

**Experimental Study 5 (preregistered, N=238):** Researchers experimentally induced uncertainty via a recall task. Results showed that under uncertainty, participants showed a stronger preference for demographically similar others. This effect was moderated by NFC: the uncertainty manipulation did not affect low-NFC individuals, but among high-NFC individuals, uncertainty significantly increased preference for similar others. A significant three-way interaction (condition × similarity × NFC) was found for demographic similarity.

**Key conclusions:** The motivation to reduce uncertainty causally shapes social network composition. High-NFC individuals prefer homophilous interactions, especially under uncertainty. This has implications for understanding social support, shared reality construction, stereotype persistence, and resistance to belief change. The findings align with Socioemotional Selectivity Theory and group-centrism literature.

The researchers developed the Content Dimensions–Overton Window–Perceived Utility (COP) Model, analyzing over 10,000 COVID-19 tweets. Even when less truthful, tweets that hit the right emotional chord and felt relevant were more likely to be liked and shared.
